item.text: {"text":"Strong margins against random negatives do not establish strong catalog ranking. Sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; smaller candidate sets increasingly resemble AUC rather than top-k retrieval ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). RecSys 2025 research distinguishes sampling resolution, fidelity to full-ranking comparisons, robustness to exposure bias, and recovery of ground-truth rankings—separate reliability questions ([sampling reliability study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086)). Sequential-recommendation experiments from 2024 also found aggregate accuracy concealed head/mid/tail disparities: random training negatives favored head items, while popularity-based alternatives improved balance at an overall accuracy cost ([Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)).\n\nPractical diagnostic synthesis: use fixed training-only prefixes with their next training interaction as target; label these as in-sample diagnostics unless excluded from fitting. For each category’s single GRU4Rec model, compare target rank and HR@10 across the full eligible catalog, repeated draws of 99 unique uniform negatives, popularity-sampled candidates, and model-scored hard competitors. Keep eligibility and seen-item exclusions consistent. Record random-negative versus hardest-competitor margins, sampled-hit/full-catalog-miss frequency, and results by target popularity and history length; compute popularity from preceding training interactions only. Separate candidate-draw variability from user-bootstrap uncertainty, using identical candidate draws for paired comparisons. Treat high-scoring unobserved items as competitors, not verified dislikes. These are proposed diagnostic protocols, not reported experimental findings; retain the unchanged host macro validation HR@10 for selection, with no score fusion or evaluator changes."}
